1.title: The Messages API: Requests, Streaming and Multi-Format Input
1.text: Welcome to Module two: The Messages A P I: Requests, Streaming and Multi-Format Input. This module covers the skills claude a p i mechanics, part one: messages, streaming, vision, messages a p i data access patterns. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. The anatomy of a Messages A P I (application programming interface) request and response. Why the A P I is stateless and how multi-turn conversations work. Streaming: the event sequence and how to assemble the result. Multi-format input: images, P D F s and the Files A P I, with their limits. The usage fields and the stop reason values.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater's First Call
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater's First Call. An adjuster asks: "Summarize claim four thousand four hundred seventy-one and list any missing documents.". The developer sends the policy text and the claim notes to Claude and wants the answer in two seconds. The same adjuster then asks a follow-up question.

1.title: A Request and Its Response
1.text: A Request and Its Response. The figure shows this: Messages A P I anatomy: the request carries model, max tokens, system and messages; the response carries content blocks, stop reason and usage.

1.title: A Request and Its Response, continued
1.text: A Request and Its Response, continued. model. The model I D (a pinned snapshot on current models). max tokens. Required; a cap on the output length. If reached, the reply is cut off and stop reason is max tokens. system. A separate parameter for instructions and context; it is not a message role. messages. A list of user and assistant turns; content can be text or blocks (text, image, document, tool use, tool result). Response content. A list of blocks: text, tool use, thinking and others. stop reason. end turn, max tokens, stop sequence, tool use, pause turn, refusal.

1.title: A Request and Its Response, continued
1.text: A Request and Its Response, continued. usage. input tokens, output tokens, and the cache fields (Module three); use it for cost tracking.

1.title: A Request and Its Response, continued
1.text: A Request and Its Response, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Stateless, so you resend the conversation
1.text: Stateless, so you resend the conversation. The A P I remembers nothing between requests. For a follow-up question, send the whole conversation so far (earlier user and assistant turns) plus the new question. The context window is everything the model can see in one request, including its own reply. It grows with every turn, so long conversations need management (Module nine). Log the request-id response header of every call: it is the key for support and for tracing (Module sixteen). Exam tip: "The model forgot what the user said earlier" in an A P I application means the history was not sent again, not that the model is faulty. Exam tip: The A P I is stateless: a follow-up that "forgot" earlier turns means the history was not resent.

1.title: Streaming
1.text: Streaming. With stream: true, the response arrives as server-sent events (S S E) so the user sees text while the model is still writing. It improves perceived latency; total time is about the same.

1.title: Streaming, continued
1.text: Streaming, continued. The figure shows this: The streaming event order: message start, content blocks with deltas, message delta, message stop; pings and errors can appear in between.

1.title: Streaming, continued
1.text: Streaming, continued. message start. A message object with empty content. content block start or content block delta or content block stop. One content block: text arrives as text delta, tool input as input json delta (partial Jason (Java Script Object Notation)), thinking as thinking delta. message delta. Top-level changes: stop reason and cumulative usage. message stop. The end. ping. Keep-alive; ignore. error. The A P I can send an error mid-stream, for example overloaded error. Assemble text by appending deltas. For a tool call, collect the partial Jason and parse it when the block stops, not before. Handle an error event by retrying or reporting, keeping the partial output only if it is useful. A stream that ends without message stop is incomplete.

1.title: Streaming, continued
1.text: Streaming, continued. Use streaming for chat and long outputs; for background jobs a normal call or a batch is simpler.

1.title: Multi-Format Input: Images and PDFs
1.text: Multi-Format Input: Images and P D F s. Image. How to provide it: Base sixty-four in the request, a U R L (uniform resource locator), or a file id from the Files A P I (upload once, reference many times). Limits and notes: Up to eight thousand by eight thousand pixels per image; many images per request (up to six hundred) but the request size limit (one hundred twenty-eight megabytes on the first-party A P I) can be reached first; large images are resized and cost visual tokens; on Amazon Bedrock and Google-managed Vertex only base sixty-four is available.

1.title: Multi-Format Input: Images and PDFs, continued
1.text: Multi-Format Input: Images and P D F s, continued. P D F. How to provide it: A document block (base sixty-four, U R L or file). Limits and notes: Each page is converted to an image plus extracted text; up to six hundred pages per request (one hundred when the context window is under one million); dense P D F s can fill the context first. Text. How to provide it: Text blocks. Limits and notes: Put long documents before the question; wrap them with clear tags.

1.title: Multi-Format Input: Images and PDFs, continued
1.text: Multi-Format Input: Images and P D F s, continued. The figure shows this: Multi-format input: images and P D F s are content blocks in the user message; the Files A P I lets you upload once and reference many times. Token cost of images and P D F s counts toward the context window and the bill; check with the token counting endpoint before sending large files. Large or repeated files: use the Files A P I instead of resending base sixty-four on every turn.

1.title: Multi-Format Input: Images and PDFs, continued
1.text: Multi-Format Input: Images and P D F s, continued. Quality tips: place images before the text instruction, make each image legible (resolution), and label multiple images. Current documentation: six hundred images or six hundred P D F pages per request, one hundred twenty-eight megabytes request limit, eight thousand pixel maximum edge, file id through the Files A P I. These limits and the supported formats change; check the vision and P D F pages. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: Large files and many images: check token cost and limits, and use the Files A P I to upload once and reference many times.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Request: model, max tokens (required), system (separate), messages (user and assistant), optional tools, thinking, output settings. Response: content blocks, stop reason, usage. Stateless: Resend the history every request; log request-id. stop reason: end turn, max tokens, stop sequence, tool use, pause turn, refusal. Streaming: S S E: message start, block start or delta or stop, message delta (cumulative usage), message stop, ping, error. Images: base sixty-four, U R L or file id; at most eight thousand times eight thousand px; resized; visual tokens; Bedrock base sixty-four only. P D F: Page image plus text; at most six hundred pages (one hundred under a one million window). Files A P I: Upload once, reference many times.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A chat application sends only the newest user message each turn, and Claude cannot answer follow-ups that refer to earlier turns. What is the cause and the fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The A P I is stateless, so every request must carry the earlier turns.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which parameter is required in every Messages A P I request, besides the model and messages? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. max tokens is required in every request because it caps the output length; the others are optional parameters.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A response ends mid-sentence with stop reason: "max tokens". What happened? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. max tokens means the output limit was reached and the answer is incomplete.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Where does the system prompt go in a Messages A P I request? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The system prompt is its own parameter; message roles are user and assistant.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. An assistant must show text as soon as it is generated. What should the developer enable? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Streaming returns server-sent events so text can be shown incrementally.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. While streaming a tool call, the application tries to parse the tool input after the first input json delta and fails. What should it do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Tool input arrives as partial Jason that is complete only at the end of the block.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A request sends a four hundred fifty-page P D F and fails or is truncated although it is under the page limit. What is a likely cause and remedy? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Each page costs text and image tokens, so dense P D F s can exhaust the context before the page limit.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. The same twenty megabytes image is needed in every turn of a long conversation. Which approach reduces overhead? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. The Files A P I lets you upload once and reference many times.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Select two. Which two statements about the Messages A P I are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. The A P I is stateless and returns usage; streaming improves perceived latency, not total time.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all nine answers. Question one: B. Question two: D. Question three: A. Question four: A. Question five: A. Question six: D. Question seven: C. Question eight: C. Question nine: A and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
